abstracts.abstract: We propose a novel theoretical framework for analyzing the generalization capability of learning algorithms under non-i.i.d. data assumptions, addressing a fundamental limitation in classical learning theory. While traditional PAC learning theory relies critically on the i.i.d. assumption, real-world machine learning applications frequently involve temporally or spatially dependent data streams. Our framework introduces a unified analysis paradigm based on mixingale theory and stochastic approximation, establishing new generalization bounds that seamlessly bridge the gap between dependent data and standard learning guarantees. Specifically, we derive deviation inequalities for α-mixing sequences by exploiting the sequential dependence structure through mixing coefficients, demonstrating how the learning rate and effective sample size must be jointly calibrated to account for temporal correlations. The key theoretical contribution lies in establishing that the classic bias-variance decomposition remains valid under weak dependence, albeit with modified constants that quantify the dependence-induced complexity penalty. Our bounds recover known i.i.d. results as special cases while providing strictly tighter guarantees for dependent data. The framework enables principled algorithm selection for online learning and reinforcement learning domains where sample dependencies are inherent, fundamentally extending the applicability of learning theory beyond the i.i.d. paradigm.

We present a significantly refined analysis of variational Bayesian inference for latent variable models, resolving a fundamental tension between approximation quality and computational tractability that has limited practical applicability. While mean-field variational inference provides an efficient optimization framework, its empirical performance often falls short of theoretical predictions due to the overly restrictive independence assumptions on posterior approximations. We introduce a hierarchical variational family that relaxes the mean-field constraint through a structured covariance parameterization derived from the natural gradient geometry of the exponential family. Our analysis establishes new finite-sample bounds on the gap between the variational objective and the true marginal likelihood, demonstrating that the proposed family achieves faster convergence rates by exploiting curvature information in the latent space. The theoretical improvements are achieved without increasing computational complexity beyond standard mean-field methods. We further prove that the proposed variational family enables consistent estimation of model parameters under weaker regularity conditions than those required for mean-field approximations. Experimental validation on synthetic and real datasets confirms the theoretical predictions, showing substantial improvements in posterior approximation quality and predictive accuracy for mixture models and hidden Markov models.

We introduce Modular Neural Architecture Search (MNAS), a paradigm-shifting approach to automated machine learning that constructs task-specific neural network architectures through principled module composition rather than monolithic architecture optimization. Traditional Neural Architecture Search methods treat architectures as atomic design choices, ignoring the modular structure that characterizes successful architectures across domains. MNAS addresses this limitation by defining a search space of composable neural modules with well-defined interfaces, enabling architecture discovery through optimal module selection and connection topology optimization. The framework employs a novel bi-level optimization procedure where the upper level evaluates module compositions on validation performance while the lower level performs efficient module-specific training. We design a transferable module library spanning convolutional, attention-based, and graph neural network components, enabling cross-domain architecture transfer. Extensive experiments on image classification, point cloud processing, and protein structure prediction demonstrate that MNAS discovers architectures outperforming manually designed counterparts while achieving superior transfer learning performance across related tasks. The modular paradigm enables interpretable architecture analysis and facilitates knowledge transfer between architecture instances, representing a fundamental shift in how neural network architectures are conceptualized and discovered.

We present Adaptive Kernel Approximation (AKA), a substantially improved method for scaling kernel methods to large-scale datasets by addressing the accuracy-efficiency trade-off inherent in random Fourier features. Existing approaches based on random Fourier feature expansion suffer from either excessive computational costs when high accuracy is required or poor approximation quality when efficiency is prioritized. AKA introduces a data-dependent frequency sampling strategy that adaptively allocates computational budget based on the spectral concentration of the target kernel function. The key innovation lies in learning an optimal importance distribution over frequencies that minimizes approximation error for a given feature budget, formulated as a variance minimization problem over the kernel's power spectrum. We develop an efficient gradient-based optimization procedure for learning the importance distribution, with convergence guarantees established through duality theory. The learned distribution enables provably better approximations than uniform sampling while maintaining the same computational complexity. Comprehensive experiments on kernel SVM classification, kernel ridge regression, and Gaussian process regression demonstrate that AKA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art kernel approximation methods, achieving speedups of 10-100x over exact kernel computation while preserving statistical performance comparable to full kernel methods on datasets with up to ten million points.
